title: What time is it? — and the half that counts forward
goal: Tell the time, make appointments, and avoid the costliest mistake a learner of Bosnian can make: thinking *pola osam* means half past eight.
bekal: tell the time in both the full form and the conversational form
understand that *pola* counts forward to the next hour

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kada imamo sastanak?
dialogs.intro: Late afternoon at the office. Amina closes her laptop and turns toward Budi's desk.

lines.text: Budi, kada ti počinje kurs bosanskog?

lines.text: U sedam uveče, tri puta sedmično.

lines.id: At half past eight. Why do you ask?

lines.speaker: Amina:

lines.text: U deset i petnaest. Zapisao sam. Laku noć!

notes: ***U pola devet* means 8:30, not 9:30.** This is the costliest mistake a learner of Bosnian can make, and almost everyone makes it once. The explanation is in the warning box below — read it now, not later.

***Koliko je sati?* is literally "how many hours is it?"** with *sati* in the genitive plural, because *koliko* is always followed by the genitive (unit 8). The answer may use *sati* or not: *Pet sati je* and *Pet je* are both correct, the second more casual.

***Za deset minuta* = in ten minutes.** The preposition *za* has two very different jobs: with people it means "for" (*za tebe*), with time it means "in, within" (*za pet minuta, za sat vremena*). Its opposite: *prije deset minuta* = ten minutes ago.

***Nemoj kasniti!* — "don't be late!"** Prohibitions in Bosnian are formed with *nemoj* (to one person) or *nemojte* (polite/plural) followed by the dictionary form. *Nemoj zaboraviti!* (don't forget!), *Nemojte brinuti!* (don't worry!). This form is used far more often than an ordinary negative command.

**Punctuality in Bosnia has two faces.** For official matters — meetings, doctor's appointments, trains — people are on time and expect the same. For coffee with friends, *u pet* means "around five", and turning up a quarter of an hour later won't draw any comment. The word that marks the difference: *tačno* (exactly). *Tačno u pet* means five o'clock sharp.

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: Two systems live side by side: the conversational one (1-12 with *ujutro*, *popodne*, *uveče*) and the official 24-hour one for written schedules. This table covers the first.
after: **After the half hour, Bosnian counts down with *do* (to).** *Dvadeset do osam* = twenty minutes to eight = 7:40. Exactly like English *twenty to eight* — word for word.

**The word *sat* has three forms that alternate with the number**, exactly the rule from unit 5: *jedan sat, dva sata, pet sati*. So *Koliko je sati?* uses the genitive plural because of *koliko*. And remember that *sat* also means "watch, clock" and "lesson" — context tells them apart.

**Adding the part of the day removes any morning/evening confusion:** *ujutro* (in the morning, roughly 5-11), *prijepodne* (late morning), *popodne* (afternoon), *uveče* (in the evening), *noću* (at night). *U sedam ujutro* and *u sedam uveče* — and that's why Budi asks *ujutro ili uveče?*

**Official timetables use the 24-hour system**, read number by number: *voz polazi u sedamnaest i trideset*. You'll see it at stations, airports, and cinemas — but you'll almost never hear it in conversation.

grammars.title: Time prepositions — and the cases they call for
body: Every time preposition uses a case you already know. Nothing is new here except the list itself.

rows: at seven, on Monday, at noon
in ten minutes, in an hour

after: ***Prije* and *za* are opposites** and both are very common: *prije pet minuta* (five minutes ago) versus *za pet minuta* (in five minutes). One looks back, one looks ahead. Mix them up and the meaning changes completely — this is one of the few A1 mistakes that can really leave someone waiting in vain.

**Working hours and opening hours always use *od … do***: *Radimo od osam do šesnaest.* On shop doors you'll see *radno vrijeme* (opening hours) followed by the times, and *neradni dan* means a day when they're closed.

***Oko* gives you useful wiggle room.** *Dolazim oko pet* (I'll come around five) sounds natural and honest, while *dolazim u pet* is a promise. Bosnians use *oko* all the time, and learning it early will save you a lot of apologies.
**Three set sentences worth learning today:** *Koliko je sati?* (what time is it?), *Kada se vidimo?* (when shall we meet?), *Nemam vremena.* (I don't have time).

blocks.title: ⚠️ Pola — the half that counts forward
items: ***Pola osam* means 7:30.** Bosnian doesn't count half past the hour that has gone by, but **halfway toward the next hour** — like German *halb acht*. So *pola devet* = 8:30, *pola dvanaest* = 11:30, *pola jedan* = 12:30.

**If you think in English ("half eight" = 8:30 in British English), you'll always be off by an hour** — and always in the same direction: late. The safest way to get used to it is to repeat the time back in numbers: *Pola devet? Znači osam i trideset?* No native speaker will find that odd; they know exactly why you're asking.
**Pola is also used for quantities**, and there it means plain "half": *pola kilograma* (half a kilo), *pola sata* (half an hour), *pola litre* (half a liter). Only *pola* + an hour counts forward.
